title: Orbital Knitwear
pitch: A visitor tunes a satellite's height, tilt and orbit shape and watches its ground track unspool across a wool-textured world map, each pass adding a ribbon of stitches wherever the camera swath reaches. Pattern cards set goals such as seeing latitudes the space station never reaches, repeating the same track every 16 days, keeping a steady local time of day, or lingering over the far north. A flat-versus-polar toggle shows how the projection decides which holes look big, while the score counts true surface area.
whyNow: Timeless: orbital geometry never goes stale. The knitting frame makes a nerdy subject cozy, and the projection toggle and daylight terminator put a map argument at the centre.

research.summary: A ground track is a map argument: one orbit is a sine wave on a flat map and a spiral seen from the pole. Research shapes the mechanic. Earth's bulge (J2) turns an orbit's plane, and at about 98 degrees and 600-700 km that turn matches the Sun's 0.9856 degrees per day, so a satellite keeps one local solar time; a two-body-plus-J2 calculation done here gives 97.79 degrees at 600 km and 98.19 degrees at 700 km, matching both sources. Landsat's 16-day cycle of 233 orbits is a literal knitting gauge: tracks about 172 km apart against a 185 km swath. The ISS inclination of 51.6 degrees fences its track and Earth's spin moves each pass about 23 degrees west. Scoring by true area matters: the band poleward of 60 degrees is a third of an equirectangular map but about 13 percent of the planet (computed here). The Molniya figures are single-sourced.

facts.claim: A sun-synchronous orbit needs its node to drift about 0.9856 degrees per day to hold one local solar time; Earth's J2 bulge supplies the drift, at about 98.2 degrees inclination for a 700 km circular orbit (NASA primer) and about 97.8 degrees near 600 km (second source).

The International Space Station orbits at 51.6 degrees inclination, so it never gets farther north or south than 51.6 degrees latitude, at roughly 370-460 km altitude in orbits of 90 to 93 minutes; each pass lands about 22.9 degrees of longitude west of the last (NASA tutorial).

Landsat 4-9 fly a circular sun-synchronous orbit near 705 km on a 16-day repeat of 233 orbits; an orbit takes about 98.9 minutes, successive tracks sit about 24.7 degrees (2752 km) apart at the equator, and the design swath is 185 km.

Computed here from the Landsat figures: 233 evenly spaced tracks put neighbours about 172 km apart at the equator (40,075 km divided by 233), so a 185 km swath overlaps its neighbour by about 13 km, roughly 7 percent.
Molniya orbits are reported to use a critical inclination of about 63.4 degrees with a 12-hour period and two apogees per day (single source, unconfirmed).

design.coreLoop: A round starts from a pattern card with a target and a par. The visitor sets up to three satellites (altitude, inclination, eccentricity, start longitude, swath), starts the clock and fast-forwards days of orbits while stitches fill the fabric. A live panel scores true-area coverage, dropped stitches, overlap waste, revisit time and local solar time under the satellite. Small altitude changes shift the track spacing, so a gappy weave snaps into a tight repeat; every setup is a shareable link.
sophisticationHooks: Two-body propagation with J2 node and perigee drift, Kepler's equation by Newton iteration, Earth rotation and a sun model, so sun-synchronous and Molniya-style orbits emerge from physics instead of presets.
Repeat-ground-track finder: scans altitudes for k orbits in m days and marks stitch-perfect heights on the altitude slider, as in Landsat's 233 orbits per 16 days.

Projection honesty: one coverage grid renders in equirectangular and polar azimuthal views by inverse projection, while every score uses cos(latitude) area weights and a live readout shows map share versus planet share.
Pattern cards with par values from an in-page brute-force search, plus a day/night terminator so dawn-dusk orbits can ride the edge of night.
design.scopeForOneDay: Eight disjoint files: orbit engine with J2, coverage grid (Worker), projections, land and city data, wool renderer, pattern cards with par search, planner UI, app shell with hash state and about panel. Built: 8 cards, flat and polar views, terminator, true-area scoring, light and dark themes, reduced-motion mode. Left out: real satellite catalogs, atmospheric drag, 3D globe, multiplayer.
risks: Coastlines are hand-simplified from memory and may look crude; styling them as embroidered outlines with city dots keeps orientation honest.
The single-sourced Molniya figures show as 'as of 2026-10-11, per arXiv 2007.04341', though 63.4 degrees also follows from arcsin(2/sqrt 5).
Two-body plus J2 is not a precision propagator; the about panel says tracks drift from real satellites over weeks, and unit tests check the sourced figures within about 1 percent.
Pattern-card pars have to be solvable; the brute-force search verifies each card before it ships.
Wool texture at 1-degree resolution risks dropped frames on phones; an offscreen cached layer and a coarser grid on small screens mitigate this.
